[Issue #8389] Add approvals to workflow logic (#8582)

## Summary
Fixes #8389 

## Changes proposed
* Add approval support to workflow logic, including supporting multiple
different types of approvals, with varying amounts required in that
workflow.
* Add a way to generate the state machine diagrams via a script (helps
visualize what is going on here).

## Context for reviewers
There's a lot of little changes to pipe data around that is needed that
somewhat bloat the size of this PR, but if you're looking for what to
focus on:
* The state machine definition and how approval states are connected
* The approval processor itself, as well as how it connects to
everything

First, a crash course in approvals. Approvals have 3 "approval response
types" of `approved`, `declined`, `requires_modification` which will
affect how the state of the state machine needs to change. Broadly,
approved means it can potentially move onto the next state. Declined
will move it to some sort of end state (also called declined in this
case) and requires modification moves it earlier in the flow. These
aren't hard requirements, we could adjust how this all works (could make
declined and requires modification go to the same place), but that's how
I've setup the prototype.

On the state machine side to do this we need to check the approval
response type and map it to these transitions. This is done via this
chunk of code:

```py
    ## Program officer approvals
    receive_program_officer_approval = Event(
        # If Approved -> Add approval event and then check if enough approvals have occurred to determine next state
        states.PENDING_PROGRAM_OFFICER_APPROVAL.to.itself(
            cond=WorkflowConstants.IS_APPROVAL_EVENT_APPROVED,
            on=WorkflowConstants.ON_AGENCY_APPROVAL_APPROVED,
            after="check_program_officer_approval",
        )
        |
        # If Declined -> Add approval event and move to Declined state
        states.PENDING_PROGRAM_OFFICER_APPROVAL.to(
            states.DECLINED,
            cond=WorkflowConstants.IS_APPROVAL_EVENT_DECLINED,
            on=WorkflowConstants.ON_AGENCY_APPROVAL_DECLINED,
        )
        |
        # If Requires Modification -> Add approval event and move back to Start
        states.PENDING_PROGRAM_OFFICER_APPROVAL.to(
            states.START,
            cond=WorkflowConstants.IS_APPROVAL_EVENT_REQUIRES_MODIFICATION,
            on=WorkflowConstants.ON_AGENCY_APPROVAL_REQUIRES_MODIFICATION,
        )
    )

    check_program_officer_approval = Event(
        # If it has enough approvals, go to the Budget officer approval
        states.PENDING_PROGRAM_OFFICER_APPROVAL.to(
            states.PENDING_BUDGET_OFFICER_APPROVAL, cond=WorkflowConstants.HAS_ENOUGH_APPROVALS
        )
        # If not, stay in this state
        | states.PENDING_PROGRAM_OFFICER_APPROVAL.to.itself(),
    )
```
The defines a few things:
* What are the transitions. There are actually 4 transitions here off of
2 events. Declined/Requires Modification move if that conditional is
satisfied. If it is Approved, it says to run a different event after
which checks that there are enough approvals. This is necessary because
we have to first add the approval event to the DB before we can check
which state it goes to.
* Any "on" handlers, these are where the logic is actually defined, and
these alongside the conditionals are all defined in the BaseStateMachine
class (ie. we can reuse this pattern for all approvals).

Note that it is very boilerplatey, I'm think that in the future we'll
make a utility for generating this that is a bit less verbose, but want
to see how things evolve before I do that. An important detail to be
aware of, `cond` / `on` / `after` always refer to a function defined in
the state machine class itself, in this case they're all defined in the
base state machine for reusability.

---

As for approvals, most of that logic is just validation that you can do
the approval and it makes sense to do it. After that it's mainly just
adding an approval record to the DB. I can imagine a lot more we could
expand in that logic, but let's keep it (relatively) simple for now.

---

To give a step-by-step guide to how the state machine handles an event.
Let's assume we receive the event `receive_program_officer_approval`
with an approval response type of `approved`.
* The state machine will take in that event and see it has several
transitions defined in the `receive_program_officer_approval` event. It
will look at the conditionals in order to figure out which transition to
run. In this case, the conditional will see the approval response type
is `approved`, so we do the first one.
* It then runs the `on` function which is the approval processor code
and writes the approval event to the approval table.
* It then sees that there is an `after` defined and will send another
event of `check_program_officer_approval`.
* That other event also has a conditional which queries the DB and
checks the number of approvals of that type against what is required
* Assuming enough approvals are configured, it finally transitions to
the `end` state


## Validation steps
All of it is in the unit tests still at this phase as we haven't
connected to the service yet.

Note that it is very boilerplatey, I'm think that in the future we'll
make a utility for generating this that is a bit less verbose, but want
to see how things evolve before I do that. An important detail to be
aware of, `cond` / `on` / `after` always refer to a function defined in
the state machine class itself, in this case they're all defined in the
base state machine for reusability.

---

As for approvals, most of that logic is just validation that you can do
the approval and it makes sense to do it. After that it's mainly just
adding an approval record to the DB. I can imagine a lot more we could
expand in that logic, but let's keep it (relatively) simple for now.

---

To give a step-by-step guide to how the state machine handles an event.
Let's assume we receive the event `receive_program_officer_approval`
with an approval response type of `approved`.
* The state machine will take in that event and see it has several
transitions defined in the `receive_program_officer_approval` event. It
will look at the conditionals in order to figure out which transition to
run. In this case, the conditional will see the approval response type
is `approved`, so we do the first one.
* It then runs the `on` function which is the approval processor code
and writes the approval event to the approval table.
* It then sees that there is an `after` defined and will send another
event of `check_program_officer_approval`.
* That other event also has a conditional which queries the DB and
checks the number of approvals of that type against what is required
* Assuming enough approvals are configured, it finally transitions to
the `end` state

connected to the service yet.
